newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - U.S. markets confounded by murky jobs data.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - U.S. markets confounded by murky jobs data.

text.p: The U.S. employment report, which consistently gives markets a sharp jolt in one direction or the other, left bonds, stocks and the dollar struggling in search of direction on Friday after sending a slew of mixed signals.
Seizing on a weaker-than-expected headline figure and declines in the workweek and average hourly earnings, Treasuries jumped higher in the immediate aftermath of the April payrolls report's release.

But traders soon turned their attention to a surprisingly sharp fall in the unemployment rate, which fell to its lowest level since 1973 and to a threshold which economists said could prompt more pre-emptive action from the Federal Reserve later this month.
"This is a report with something for everyone," said David Blitzer, chief economist at rating agency Standard & Poor's.
By 1025 EDT/1425 GMT, Treasuries had given up all their gains and turned negative across the yield curve.
The Dow industrials, meanwhile, gleaned some strength from the payrolls report and climbed close to 50 points early, before paring their gains.
The Labor Department reported on Friday that the U.S. economy added 142,000 nonfarm jobs in April, substantially lower than Wall Street consensus forecasts for a gain of 211,000.
The average workweek declined to 34.6 hours from 34.9 hours in March, while average hourly earnings slipped to $12.14 from $12.15 in the prior month.
The real shocker, however, was the decline in the jobless rate, which fell 0.3 percentage points to 4.9 percent, a level which many market participants fear could unleash inflationary pressures.
"With the exception of the drop in the unemployment rate, the jobs numbers were unambiguously good," said Jeffrey Applegate, chief investment strategist, Lehman Brothers.
"The stock market is doing well, but it's not flying because of that number," he added. "By most peoples' notions that would put us close to full employment."
